function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **complete set of files** you’ll need to add to the `nodejs-welcome` repository so that it can be built, deployed to Kubernetes, and automatically built on every push to `main`.  
I’ve also included the exact shell commands you can run locally (or in a CI job) to commit and push the changes.

> **NOTE** – I’m assuming the repository is already cloned locally at `~/nodejs-welcome`.  
> If you’re running this from a fresh machine, replace `~/nodejs-welcome` with the absolute path to your clone.

---

## 1️⃣  Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` in the root of the repo with the following content:

```dockerfile
# Use the official Node.js 18 slim image as the base
FROM node:18-slim

# Set the working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy package.json and package-lock.json first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the application source
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the application
CMD ["npm", "start"]
```

> *Why Node 18?*  
> The latest LTS release (18.x) is stable and includes many performance improvements.  
> Feel free to change the tag if you need a different Node version.

---

## 2️⃣  Kubernetes YAML

Create a file named `k8s-deployment.yaml` in the root of the repo with the following content:

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- update with your registry & tag
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
        env:
        - name: NODE_ENV
          value: production
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **What to change?**  
> * `image:` – Replace `ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest` with the actual image you’ll push to your registry (e.g., Docker Hub, GitHub Container Registry, etc.).  
> * `replicas:` – Adjust the number of pods to suit your load.  
> * `type:` – `LoadBalancer` works on most cloud providers; switch to `NodePort` or `ClusterIP` if you’re on a bare‑metal cluster.

---

## 3️⃣  GitHub Actions Workflow

Create a file named `.github/workflows/ci.yml` in the root of the repo with the following content:

```yaml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  build-and-push:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write   # Needed for pushing to GHCR

    steps:
    - name: Checkout repository
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

    - name: Log in to GitHub Container Registry
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        registry: ghcr.io
        username: ${{ github.actor }}
        password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Build and push Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        file: ./Dockerfile
        push: true
        tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest

    - name: Deploy to Kubernetes (optional)
      # Uncomment and configure if you want to deploy automatically
      # uses: azure/k8s-deploy@v3
      # with:
      #   manifests: k8s-deployment.yaml
      #   kubeconfig: ${{ secrets.KUBECONFIG }}
```

> **What to enable?**  
> * The `Deploy to Kubernetes` step is commented out because you’ll need a `KUBECONFIG` secret in the repo’s settings.  
> * If you prefer to keep deployments manual, leave it commented.

---

## 4️⃣  Add, Commit, Push

Open a terminal, navigate to the repo, and run:

```bash
cd ~/nodejs-welcome

# Stage the new files
git add Dockerfile k8s-deployment.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml

# Commit with a descriptive message
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"

# Push to the remote
git push origin main
```

> If you’re on a fork, replace `origin` with the name of your fork remote (e.g., `upstream`).

---

## 5️⃣  Verify

Once pushed, GitHub Actions will automatically trigger the workflow.  
Check the **Actions** tab to confirm that the image was built and pushed successfully.  
If you enabled the deployment step, verify that the pods are running:

```bash
kubectl get pods -l app=nodejs-welcome
kubectl get svc nodejs-welcome-service
```

---

### Recap

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `Dockerfile` | Builds a lightweight Node.js image |
| `k8s-deployment.yaml` | Deploys the app to Kubernetes with a LoadBalancer service |
| `.github/workflows/ci.yml` | Automates Docker build/push on pushes to `main` |

Feel free to tweak the values (image tags, replica counts, service type, etc.) to match your environment. Happy coding!
